problem_description: Build a counter component that supports increment, decrement, and reset operations using the useState hook. The counter should not go below zero. Display the current count prominently, and disable the decrement button when the count is zero. Additionally, change the text color to red when the count exceeds 10.
problem_hints: Think about which hook manages local component state and how to initialize it.
Use conditional logic in the button's disabled prop and inline styles or className toggling for the color change.
useState returns [value, setter]. Use Math.max(0, count - 1) to prevent negatives, and a ternary on count > 10 for styling.

problem_rubric.description: Correctly uses useState to track count, initializes to 0, and updates immutably.
Increment, decrement, and reset all work correctly. Decrement does not go below 0.
Decrement button is disabled at zero. Color changes to red when count exceeds 10.
Clean component structure, proper JSX, no unnecessary re-renders or state.

problem_description: Create a controlled form component with fields for name, email, and message. Implement real-time validation: name must be at least 2 characters, email must match a basic email regex, and message must be at least 10 characters. Display inline error messages beneath each field as the user types. Disable the submit button until all fields are valid.
problem_hints: Controlled components store their values in state and update via onChange handlers.
Create a validation function that runs on every state change and returns an errors object keyed by field name.
Use a useEffect or derive validation state from the current form values on each render. The submit button's disabled prop should check that the errors object has no entries.

problem_rubric.description: All three fields are properly controlled via state with onChange handlers.
Name length, email regex, and message length validations are correct and run in real-time.
Inline error messages appear beneath the correct fields and disappear when valid.
Submit button is disabled when any field is invalid and enabled only when all pass.

problem_description: Build a Todo List application where users can add, toggle complete, and delete todos. Each todo should display its text with a strikethrough when completed. Persist the todo list to localStorage so it survives page refreshes. Include an input field with an Add button, and each todo item should have a checkbox and a delete button.
problem_hints: You will need useState for the list and useEffect for syncing with localStorage.
On mount, read from localStorage and parse the JSON. On every state update to todos, write back to localStorage.
Use JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('todos')) || [] for initialization, and a useEffect with [todos] dependency to persist.

problem_rubric.description: Add, toggle, and delete operations all work correctly on the todo list.
Todos are saved to localStorage on change and loaded on mount.
Completed todos show strikethrough. Checkbox reflects completion state.
Cannot add empty todos. Handles empty localStorage gracefully.

problem_description: Create a reusable Modal component that uses React Portals to render outside the main DOM hierarchy. The modal should accept children, an isOpen prop, and an onClose callback. It must render into a dedicated div#modal-root element. Clicking the backdrop (overlay) should close the modal, but clicking inside the modal content should not. Include a close button in the top-right corner.
problem_hints: React Portals are created with ReactDOM.createPortal(child, container).
Use event.stopPropagation() on the modal content div to prevent backdrop click from firing when clicking inside.
Ensure div#modal-root exists in your HTML. Render the overlay with an onClick={onClose} and the inner content with onClick={e => e.stopPropagation()}.

problem_rubric.description: Modal renders via ReactDOM.createPortal into a separate DOM node.
Modal shows/hides based on isOpen prop. onClose fires on backdrop click and close button.
Clicking inside modal content does not trigger close. Only backdrop and close button do.
Component accepts children and is generic enough to wrap any content.

problem_description: Build a searchable, filterable list component. Given an array of product objects (with name, category, and price fields), render a list that can be filtered by a search term (matching name) and by category via a dropdown. Both filters should work simultaneously. Display the count of matching results above the list. If no results match, show a friendly empty state message.
problem_hints: Derive the filtered list from state rather than storing filtered results separately.
Use two pieces of state: searchTerm and selectedCategory. Filter the products array using both on each render.
Chain .filter() calls: first filter by category (if not 'all'), then by whether name.toLowerCase().includes(searchTerm.toLowerCase()).

problem_rubric.description: Search and category filters work correctly both independently and together.
Filtered list is computed from source data + filter state, not stored separately.
Search input, category dropdown, result count, and empty state all render correctly.
Clean separation of concerns, no unnecessary state, readable code.

problem_description: Create a set of accordion/collapsible components where only one section can be open at a time. The Accordion component should accept an array of items, each with a title and content. Clicking a section title should expand it and collapse any previously open section. Include smooth CSS transitions for the expand/collapse animation. Add an aria-expanded attribute for accessibility.
problem_hints: Track which section is open using a single piece of state (the index or id of the open item).
For smooth transitions, use max-height with CSS transition rather than display:none toggling.
Set the open index on click. If the clicked index matches the current open index, set it to null (close all). Use aria-expanded={isOpen} on each trigger button.

problem_rubric.description: Only one section is expanded at a time. Clicking an open section collapses it.
Expand/collapse uses CSS transitions and looks smooth.
aria-expanded is set correctly. Trigger elements are buttons or have proper roles.
Accordion accepts items as props and is reusable with any content.

problem_description: Build a custom useDebounce hook that delays updating a value until a specified delay has passed since the last change. Then use this hook to implement a search input that only triggers an API call (simulated with console.log or a mock function) after the user stops typing for 500ms. Display a loading indicator while the debounced value is pending, and show the final debounced value below the input.
problem_hints: useDebounce should use useState and useEffect internally, with a setTimeout that resets on each value change.
In the useEffect, set a timeout that updates the debounced value after the delay. Return a cleanup function that clears the timeout.
const [debouncedValue, setDebouncedValue] = useState(value); useEffect(() => { const timer = setTimeout(() => setDebouncedValue(value), delay); return () => clearTimeout(timer); }, [value, delay]);

problem_rubric.description: useDebounce correctly delays value updates using setTimeout with proper cleanup.
Search input uses the hook and triggers the mock API call only after debounce.
Loading indicator shows while input value differs from debounced value.
Timeout is properly cleared on unmount and on value change to prevent memory leaks.

problem_description: Implement a theme system using React Context API. Create a ThemeProvider that supports at least three themes (light, dark, and high-contrast). Each theme should define colors for background, text, primary, secondary, and border. Components nested at any depth should be able to consume the current theme and a toggleTheme function. Build a demo page with a navbar, card, and button that all respond to theme changes. Persist the selected theme to localStorage.
problem_hints: Create a ThemeContext with createContext. The provider should hold the current theme name in state and expose both the theme object and a cycle/set function.
Define a themes object mapping theme names to color objects. Use useEffect to sync the selected theme name to localStorage and read it on mount.
Consuming components can use useContext(ThemeContext) to get { theme, setTheme }. Apply theme colors via inline styles or CSS variables set on :root.

problem_rubric.description: ThemeContext is properly created with provider and consumer pattern.
At least 3 themes with 5+ color properties each, well-structured.
Multiple nested components correctly consume and react to theme changes.
Selected theme survives page refresh via localStorage.
Navbar, card, and button all visually respond to theme switching.

problem_description: Build a data fetching component that displays a paginated list of users from a mock API. Implement loading, error, and empty states. Use useReducer to manage the complex state (users array, current page, total pages, loading boolean, error string). Include Previous/Next pagination buttons that trigger new fetches. Add a retry button on error state. The component should cancel in-flight requests when a new page is requested or the component unmounts.
problem_hints: useReducer is ideal here because you have multiple related state values that change together (loading, data, error, page).
Define action types like FETCH_START, FETCH_SUCCESS, FETCH_ERROR, SET_PAGE. Use an AbortController to cancel pending fetch calls.

Create the AbortController in the useEffect, pass its signal to fetch, and return () => controller.abort() as cleanup. Dispatch FETCH_START before fetching, then FETCH_SUCCESS or FETCH_ERROR based on the result.

problem_rubric.description: Reducer handles all state transitions with clear action types and immutable updates.
Fetches data on page change, handles loading/success/error correctly.
AbortController cancels in-flight requests on page change and unmount.
Previous/Next buttons work, are disabled at boundaries, and show current page.
Error state renders with message and retry button that re-triggers the fetch.

problem_description: Create a multi-step form wizard with 3 steps: Personal Info (name, email), Address (street, city, zip), and Review & Submit. Implement forward and backward navigation between steps. Validate each step before allowing the user to proceed to the next. On the Review step, display all entered data and a submit button. Use useContext to share form state across step components. Show a progress bar indicating the current step out of total steps.
problem_hints: Create a FormContext that holds all field values and a dispatch or update function. Each step component reads/writes from this shared context.
Track the current step index in the parent. Validation should run when clicking Next -- if it fails, show errors and block navigation.
The progress bar width can be calculated as ((currentStep + 1) / totalSteps) * 100 + '%'. The Review step simply reads all values from context and displays them.

problem_rubric.description: Forward and backward navigation works. Step components mount/unmount correctly.
Form data is shared via context, accessible from all steps without prop drilling.
Each step validates its fields before allowing Next. Errors are displayed inline.
Review step shows all data correctly. Submit button triggers final action.
Progress bar accurately reflects current step out of total steps.

problem_description: Build a drag-and-drop Kanban board with three columns: To Do, In Progress, and Done. Users should be able to drag task cards between columns using the HTML5 Drag and Drop API (no external libraries). Each card shows a title and priority badge. Track the state of all tasks in a single array with a status field. Reorder should update state immediately and the UI should reflect the new positions.
problem_hints: Use onDragStart, onDragOver (with preventDefault), and onDrop events on the card and column elements.
Store a dragging item reference in state or a ref. On drop, update that item's status field to match the target column.
Set dataTransfer.setData('text/plain', taskId) on drag start. On drop, read it back and update the tasks array by mapping over it and changing the status of the matching task.

problem_rubric.description: Cards can be dragged between all three columns using native HTML5 DnD API.
Single source of truth array updated correctly on drop. No stale state.
Visual feedback during drag (cursor, highlight). Cards render in correct columns.
Clean event handler logic, proper key props, no unnecessary re-renders.

problem_description: Implement an infinite scroll feed component that loads batches of posts as the user scrolls near the bottom of the page. Use the Intersection Observer API via a custom useIntersectionObserver hook. Each post should display a title, body preview, and author. Show a loading spinner at the bottom while fetching. Handle the case where all posts have been loaded by showing an end-of-list message and stopping further observations.
problem_hints: Create a sentinel div at the bottom of the list. When it enters the viewport, trigger the next fetch.
Your custom hook should accept a ref and options, create an IntersectionObserver, and return isIntersecting. Clean up the observer on unmount.
Track a hasMore boolean. When the API returns fewer items than the page size, set hasMore to false and disconnect the observer.

problem_rubric.description: useIntersectionObserver correctly wraps the API, observes the target, and cleans up.
New batches load automatically when scrolling near bottom. Data appends correctly.
Stops fetching when no more data. Shows end-of-list message.
Spinner shows during fetch. No duplicate fetches for the same page.
Each post displays title, body preview, and author correctly.

problem_description: Build a real-time chat interface component. Messages should appear in a scrollable container that auto-scrolls to the bottom when new messages arrive. Implement a message input with send button and Enter key support. Each message should show the sender name, message text, and timestamp. Use useRef to manage the scroll container and auto-scroll behavior. Include a 'scroll to bottom' floating button that appears when the user scrolls up and disappears when at the bottom.
problem_hints: Use a ref on the messages container. After new messages are added to state, call containerRef.current.scrollTop = containerRef.current.scrollHeight.
Track whether the user is scrolled up by comparing scrollTop + clientHeight to scrollHeight in an onScroll handler.
Only auto-scroll if the user was already at the bottom before the new message arrived. Show the floating button when they are not at the bottom.

problem_rubric.description: Messages render with sender, text, and formatted timestamp in a scrollable container.
Container auto-scrolls to bottom on new messages only when user is already at bottom.
Send button and Enter key both submit. Input clears after send. Cannot send empty.
Floating button appears when scrolled up, clicking it scrolls to bottom, then it hides.
Refs used correctly for DOM access. No direct DOM manipulation outside refs.

problem_description: Create an ErrorBoundary class component that catches JavaScript errors in its child component tree. It should display a fallback UI with the error message and a 'Try Again' button that resets the boundary. Implement componentDidCatch to log errors to a mock error reporting service. Also create a useErrorHandler custom hook for functional components that can programmatically trigger the nearest error boundary. Test it with a component that throws on a button click.
problem_hints: Error boundaries must be class components using static getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch lifecycle methods.
getDerivedStateFromError returns new state with hasError: true. componentDidCatch receives error and errorInfo for logging.
For the hook, throw the error from a state update: const [error, setError] = useState(null); if (error) throw error; return setError. This triggers the nearest boundary on next render.

problem_rubric.description: Properly implements getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch. Catches child errors.
Shows error message and retry button. Retry resets hasError state to re-render children.
componentDidCatch logs to a mock service with error and component stack.
Hook allows functional components to programmatically trigger the error boundary.
Demo component correctly throws and is caught. Recovery works after retry.

problem_description: Implement a virtualized list component that efficiently renders only the visible items from a large dataset of 10,000 items. Calculate which items are in the viewport based on scroll position, item height, and container height. Render only those items plus a small buffer above and below. Use absolute positioning within a tall container to maintain correct scroll behavior. Display the total item count and current visible range. Do not use any external virtualization library.
problem_hints: The outer container has overflow:auto and a fixed height. The inner container has height = totalItems * itemHeight to create the right scrollbar.
On scroll, calculate startIndex = Math.floor(scrollTop / itemHeight) and visibleCount = Math.ceil(containerHeight / itemHeight). Add a buffer of ~5 items above and below.
Render only items from (startIndex - buffer) to (startIndex + visibleCount + buffer). Position each with style={{ position: 'absolute', top: index * itemHeight }}.

problem_rubric.description: Correctly calculates visible range from scroll position. Only visible items are in the DOM.
Handles 10,000 items smoothly. DOM node count stays constant regardless of dataset size.
Scrollbar size is correct. Scrolling feels native with no jumps or flickers.
Items above and below viewport are pre-rendered to prevent flashing on fast scroll.
Shows total count and currently visible range (e.g., 'Showing 45-65 of 10,000').

problem_description: Build a complete client-side routing system from scratch without using React Router or any routing library. Implement a Router component that listens to popstate events and matches the current URL path to registered routes. Support exact and parameterized routes (e.g., /users/:id). Create Link and NavLink components that use pushState for navigation without page reloads. NavLink should apply an active class when its path matches. Implement a NotFound fallback route. Handle nested routes and a simple layout with persistent sidebar navigation.
problem_hints: Use window.addEventListener('popstate', handler) and history.pushState to manage navigation. Store the current path in state.
For parameterized routes, convert route patterns like /users/:id into regex: /^\/users\/([^/]+)$/. Extract params with match groups.
The Router component holds current path state. On mount, read window.location.pathname. Link components call history.pushState then update Router state via context or a custom event.

problem_rubric.description: Exact and parameterized routes match correctly. Params are extracted and passed to components.
Link/NavLink use pushState. No page reloads. Back/forward browser buttons work via popstate.
NavLink applies active class when current path matches its to prop.
Unmatched paths render a NotFound component.
Persistent sidebar layout with nested content area that changes based on route.

problem_description: Create a full-featured data table component with sorting, multi-column filtering, pagination, and row selection. The table should accept a columns config array (defining header, accessor key, sortable boolean, filterable boolean) and a data array. Sorting should support ascending, descending, and unsorted states with visual indicators. Filters should be per-column text inputs in the header row. Pagination should be configurable (rows per page). Row selection should use checkboxes with a select-all checkbox in the header. Export selected rows as JSON via a button.
problem_hints: Process data through a pipeline: first filter, then sort, then paginate. Derive the displayed data on each render rather than storing intermediate results.
For multi-column sorting, you could support single-column sort with a sortConfig { key, direction } state. For filters, use an object { columnKey: filterValue }.
Selection can be a Set of row IDs. Select-all toggles all currently visible (filtered+paginated) rows. The export button calls JSON.stringify on rows whose IDs are in the selection Set.

problem_rubric.description: Click column headers to cycle asc/desc/none. Visual indicators show sort state.
Per-column text filters work independently and together. Only filterable columns show inputs.
Configurable page size. Page controls work. Resets to page 1 on filter/sort change.
Checkbox per row. Select-all for current page. Selection persists across pages.
Export selected rows as JSON. Columns config drives table rendering correctly.

problem_description: Implement a state management library similar to a minimal Redux from scratch. Create a createStore function that accepts a reducer and returns { getState, dispatch, subscribe }. Then build a React integration layer: a StoreProvider component and a useSelector hook (with shallow equality check to prevent unnecessary re-renders) and a useDispatch hook. Support middleware via an applyMiddleware function that composes middleware around dispatch (implement a logger middleware and a thunk middleware for async actions). Demonstrate with a shopping cart feature that uses async actions to fetch products.
problem_hints: createStore: hold state in a closure. dispatch runs the reducer and notifies subscribers. subscribe adds a listener and returns an unsubscribe function.
useSelector should subscribe to the store on mount, and only trigger a re-render if the selected value has changed (use useRef to store previous value and shallow compare).
Middleware signature: store => next => action. applyMiddleware chains them. Thunk middleware checks if action is a function: if so, call action(dispatch, getState) instead of passing to next.

problem_rubric.description: getState, dispatch, and subscribe work correctly. Reducer produces new state immutably.
StoreProvider, useSelector, and useDispatch hooks work. Components re-render on relevant state changes only.
applyMiddleware composes correctly. Logger logs actions. Thunk enables async dispatch.
useSelector avoids re-renders when selected value is shallowly equal to previous.
Shopping cart works with async product fetching via thunk actions.

problem_description: Build a spreadsheet-like grid component that supports 100 rows and 26 columns (A-Z). Each cell should be editable on double-click, switching from display mode to an input. Implement formula support: cells starting with '=' should evaluate simple expressions like =A1+B2 or =SUM(A1:A10). When a referenced cell changes, all dependent cells should recalculate automatically. Implement cell selection with keyboard arrow key navigation. Optimize rendering so that only changed cells re-render using React.memo and careful state design.
problem_hints: Store cell data in a Map or object keyed by cell ID (e.g., 'A1'). Build a dependency graph: when cell A1 references B2, A1 depends on B2.
For formula parsing, split on operators for simple expressions. For SUM(A1:A10), parse the range and sum the values. Use a topological sort or recursive evaluation for the dependency chain.
Wrap each Cell in React.memo with a custom comparison function that only checks if that cell's value or display value changed. Use useCallback for handlers passed to cells.

problem_rubric.description: 100x26 grid renders with column headers A-Z and row numbers. Scrollable.
Double-click enters edit mode. Blur or Enter commits. Escape cancels.
= expressions evaluate. Supports basic arithmetic and SUM range function. Handles cell references.
Changing a cell triggers recalc of all dependents. No circular dependency crash.
React.memo prevents full grid re-render. Only affected cells update. Keyboard navigation works.

problem_description: Create an accessible, fully keyboard-navigable component library consisting of: a Combobox (autocomplete input with listbox), a DatePicker (calendar popup with month navigation), and a Tooltip. All components must follow WAI-ARIA authoring practices. The Combobox must support aria-activedescendant, arrow key navigation through options, Enter to select, and Escape to close. The DatePicker must use a grid role for the calendar, support arrow keys for day navigation, and announce the selected date to screen readers via aria-live. The Tooltip must use aria-describedby and appear on focus as well as hover. Implement proper focus trapping in the DatePicker popup.
problem_hints: Reference the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices for combobox, dialog, and tooltip patterns. Each has specific role, state, and property requirements.
For the Combobox, manage activeIndex state for aria-activedescendant. The listbox role container holds option role items. Arrow keys move activeIndex, Enter selects options[activeIndex].
DatePicker focus trap: on Tab at the last focusable element, move focus to the first. Use a ref to track all focusable elements inside the popup. aria-live='polite' region announces date changes.

problem_rubric.description: Correct ARIA roles/states. Keyboard navigation works. Screen reader announces options.
Grid role calendar. Arrow key day navigation. Focus trapping. aria-live announcements.
aria-describedby links trigger to tooltip. Shows on focus and hover. Dismissible with Escape.
All three components are fully operable via keyboard only. No mouse dependency.
Roles, states, and properties follow WAI-ARIA authoring practices accurately.

problem_description: Build a simple HTTP server using the net/http standard library that serves three endpoints: GET /health returns a 200 JSON response with {"status": "ok"}, GET /time returns the current server time in ISO 8601 format, and GET /echo?message=hello returns the query parameter value in a JSON response. All responses must have Content-Type: application/json header. Handle missing query parameters with a 400 Bad Request response.
problem_hints: Use http.HandleFunc to register handlers and http.ListenAndServe to start the server.
Read query parameters with r.URL.Query().Get("message"). Use json.NewEncoder(w).Encode() to write JSON responses.
Set headers before writing the response body: w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json"). For 400 errors, use w.WriteHeader(http.StatusBadRequest) before encoding the error JSON.

problem_rubric.description: All three endpoints return correct responses with proper status codes.
Responses are valid JSON with correct Content-Type header.
Missing query params return 400 with descriptive error message.
Clean handler functions, proper imports, idiomatic Go style.

problem_description: Create a CLI tool that reads a JSON configuration file, validates required fields (name, version, port), and outputs a formatted summary to stdout. The tool should accept the file path as a command-line argument. If the file doesn't exist, is not valid JSON, or is missing required fields, print a clear error message to stderr and exit with a non-zero code. Use the flag package for argument parsing and support a --verbose flag that prints additional details.
problem_hints: Use os.Args or the flag package to parse arguments. Read the file with os.ReadFile.
Unmarshal into a struct with json.Unmarshal. Check for zero values on required fields after unmarshaling.
Write errors to os.Stderr with fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, ...) and call os.Exit(1). For verbose mode, conditionally print extra fields.

problem_rubric.description: Reads file from CLI argument. Handles missing file gracefully.
Unmarshals JSON correctly. Reports parse errors clearly.
Checks all required fields. Reports which fields are missing.
Flag parsing works. Verbose mode adds detail. Proper exit codes.

problem_description: Implement a concurrent file word counter. Given a list of file paths as command-line arguments, launch a goroutine for each file to count words concurrently. Use channels to collect results and print a summary table showing each filename and its word count, plus a total. Handle errors for files that cannot be opened without crashing the program. Limit concurrency to at most 5 simultaneous goroutines using a semaphore pattern.
problem_hints: Create a buffered channel of capacity 5 to use as a semaphore. Send to it before starting work, receive from it when done.
Use a results channel of a struct type { filename string, count int, err error }. Each goroutine sends one result.
Read files with os.Open and bufio.NewScanner with scanner.Split(bufio.ScanWords). Count calls to scanner.Scan().

problem_rubric.description: Files are processed concurrently with goroutines. Semaphore limits to 5 concurrent.
Accurate word counts for each file.
Unreadable files report errors without crashing. Other files still process.
Summary table with per-file counts and total is formatted and readable.

problem_description: Build a simple in-memory key-value store exposed via a REST API. Implement PUT /store/{key} with a JSON body {"value": "..."} to set a value, GET /store/{key} to retrieve it, DELETE /store/{key} to remove it, and GET /store to list all keys. The store must be safe for concurrent access. Return 404 for keys that don't exist. Include a TTL feature: PUT requests can optionally include a ttl_seconds field, and expired entries should not be returned by GET.
problem_hints: Use sync.RWMutex to protect the map. RLock for reads, Lock for writes.
Store entries as structs with value, createdAt, and ttl fields. On GET, check if time.Now().After(createdAt.Add(ttl)).
For the list endpoint, iterate the map and skip expired entries. Consider a background goroutine with a ticker to periodically clean up expired entries.

problem_rubric.description: PUT, GET, DELETE, and list all work correctly with proper status codes.
sync.RWMutex or equivalent protects the map. No race conditions.
TTL is stored and checked on read. Expired keys return 404. Cleanup works.
404 for missing keys. 400 for bad requests. JSON error messages.

problem_description: Create a logging middleware for an HTTP server that wraps any http.Handler. For each request, the middleware should log: HTTP method, request path, response status code, response size in bytes, and request duration in milliseconds. Format the log as structured JSON written to stdout. To capture the status code and response size, you must implement a custom ResponseWriter wrapper. Chain this middleware with a CORS middleware that sets Access-Control-Allow-Origin, Allow-Methods, and Allow-Headers headers.
problem_hints: Create a struct that embeds http.ResponseWriter and adds statusCode and bytesWritten fields. Override WriteHeader and Write methods.
In the logging middleware, record time.Now() before calling next.ServeHTTP, then calculate duration after. Read captured status and size from your wrapper.
Chain middleware by having each return an http.Handler. loggingMiddleware(corsMiddleware(yourHandler)).

problem_rubric.description: Custom wrapper correctly captures status code and bytes written without breaking the response.
Structured JSON log with method, path, status, size, and duration for each request.
Sets correct CORS headers. Handles OPTIONS preflight requests.
Both middlewares compose cleanly and work with any handler.

problem_description: Write a Go package that implements a generic in-memory cache with expiration support using Go generics (type parameters). The cache should support Get, Set (with TTL), Delete, and Len operations. It must be concurrency-safe. Implement a background cleanup goroutine that runs on a configurable interval and removes expired entries. Provide a Close method that stops the cleanup goroutine using a done channel. Write table-driven unit tests covering set/get, expiration, deletion, and concurrent access.
problem_hints: Use type Cache[K comparable, V any] struct with a sync.RWMutex and map[K]entry[V] where entry has value and expiresAt.
The cleanup goroutine should select on a time.Ticker.C channel and a done channel. On tick, lock and delete expired entries. On done, return.
For tests, use t.Run with subtests. For concurrency tests, launch multiple goroutines doing Set/Get and use the -race flag.

problem_rubric.description: Uses Go generics correctly. Works with multiple types.
Mutex protects all map access. Passes race detector.
Entries expire correctly. Background goroutine cleans up. Close stops it.
Table-driven tests cover all operations including concurrent access.

problem_description: Build a URL shortener service with two endpoints: POST /shorten accepts {"url": "https://..."} and returns a short code, and GET /{code} redirects to the original URL with a 301 status. Store mappings in memory using a map. Generate short codes using a base62 encoding of an incrementing counter. Validate that submitted URLs are well-formed using net/url.Parse. Track visit counts for each short URL and expose them via GET /stats/{code}. Return appropriate errors for invalid URLs and unknown codes.
problem_hints: Base62 uses characters 0-9, a-z, A-Z. Convert the counter integer to base62 by repeatedly dividing by 62 and mapping remainders.
Use net/url.Parse(rawURL) and check that both scheme and host are non-empty to validate URLs.
For redirects, use http.Redirect(w, r, originalURL, http.StatusMovedPermanently). Increment the visit counter atomically or under a lock.

problem_rubric.description: POST creates short codes. Base62 encoding produces valid, unique codes.
GET /{code} redirects with 301. Unknown codes return 404.
Rejects malformed URLs with descriptive 400 error.
Visit count increments on each redirect. Stats endpoint returns the count.
Clean structure, proper error handling, idiomatic Go.

problem_description: Implement a token-based authentication middleware system. Create endpoints for POST /register (accept username/password, hash password with bcrypt, store in memory), POST /login (verify credentials, return a JWT token), and GET /protected (requires valid JWT in Authorization: Bearer header). The JWT should include the username, issued-at, and expiration claims. The middleware should extract the token, validate it, and inject the username into the request context. Handle expired tokens, malformed tokens, and missing headers with appropriate error responses.
problem_hints: Use golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt for password hashing: bcrypt.GenerateFromPassword and bcrypt.CompareHashAndPassword.
For JWT, use a library like github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v5. Create tokens with jwt.NewWithClaims and validate with jwt.Parse with a key function.

problem_rubric.description: Stores user with bcrypt-hashed password. Rejects duplicate usernames.
Verifies credentials. Returns signed JWT with correct claims and expiration.
Extracts Bearer token, validates JWT, injects user into context.
401 for expired/invalid/missing tokens. 400 for bad input. Clear error messages.
Passwords never stored in plain text. JWT secret is not hardcoded in handlers.

problem_description: Build a worker pool system that processes jobs from a channel. Implement a Pool struct that accepts a configurable number of workers and a job queue size. Each job is a function that returns a Result struct with an ID, output value, and error. Workers pull from the job channel, execute the function, and send results to a results channel. Implement graceful shutdown: when Stop is called, stop accepting new jobs, wait for in-flight jobs to finish, and close the results channel. Add support for job timeouts using context.WithTimeout. Include a monitor goroutine that logs pool stats (active workers, pending jobs, completed count) every N seconds.
problem_hints: Workers are goroutines in a for-range loop over the jobs channel. Closing the jobs channel signals workers to stop after draining.
Use sync.WaitGroup to track active workers. When all workers are done, close the results channel.
For timeouts, wrap each job execution in a select with ctx.Done() and the job result. The monitor goroutine uses a ticker and atomic counters.

problem_rubric.description: Configurable workers and queue size. Workers correctly consume from job channel.
Results channel receives all job outcomes. ID, value, and error are set correctly.
Stop prevents new jobs, waits for in-flight, then closes results channel.
context.WithTimeout cancels long-running jobs. Timeout errors are returned.
Stats goroutine logs active workers, pending jobs, and completion count periodically.

problem_description: Create a rate limiter middleware using the token bucket algorithm. The limiter should be configurable with requests per second and burst size. Implement per-client rate limiting based on IP address (using X-Forwarded-For header with fallback to RemoteAddr). Store client buckets in a concurrent map with automatic cleanup of stale entries. Return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header when the limit is exceeded. Write an HTTP middleware that wraps any handler. Include unit tests that verify rate limiting behavior using a mock clock or time manipulation.
problem_hints: Token bucket: each client has tokens (starts at burst). On request, check if tokens > 0. Tokens refill at rate per second based on elapsed time since last request.
Use sync.Map or a regular map with RWMutex for per-client buckets. Store lastTime and tokens per client.

Calculate tokens to add: elapsed := time.Since(bucket.lastTime); bucket.tokens = min(burst, bucket.tokens + elapsed.Seconds() * rate). Stale cleanup: periodically remove clients not seen for >10 minutes.

problem_rubric.description: Correct implementation with configurable rate and burst. Tokens refill over time.
Separate limits per IP. X-Forwarded-For and RemoteAddr handled correctly.
Middleware returns 429 with Retry-After header. Passes through when under limit.
Stale client entries are cleaned up periodically to prevent memory leaks.
Unit tests verify limiting, bursting, and recovery behavior.

problem_description: Implement a pub/sub message broker in Go. Create a Broker struct that supports Subscribe(topic) returning a channel, Unsubscribe(topic, channel), and Publish(topic, message). Messages published to a topic should be delivered to all subscribers of that topic. Subscribers that are slow (channel buffer full) should be skipped with a warning log rather than blocking the publisher. Support wildcard subscriptions where subscribing to 'events.*' receives messages published to 'events.click', 'events.scroll', etc. Include a graceful Close method that closes all subscriber channels.
problem_hints: Use a map[string][]chan Message for topic to subscriber channels. Protect with sync.RWMutex.
On Publish, iterate subscribers and use a select with default to do non-blocking sends. Log a warning if the channel is full.
For wildcards, when publishing to 'events.click', also check all subscription patterns. Use strings.HasSuffix on the pattern (stripped of '*') to match.

problem_rubric.description: Subscribe, Unsubscribe, and Publish work correctly for exact topics.
Slow subscribers are skipped, not blocking. Warning logged.
Wildcard patterns match correctly. Messages routed to wildcard subscribers.
Thread-safe operations. No panics on concurrent subscribe/publish.
Close method shuts down all channels cleanly. No goroutine leaks.

problem_description: Build a WebSocket chat server using the gorilla/websocket or nhooyr.io/websocket library. The server should support multiple chat rooms. Clients send JSON messages with {"room": "general", "username": "alice", "text": "hello"}. The server broadcasts the message to all other clients in the same room. Implement /join and /leave commands. Maintain a list of active users per room and broadcast user join/leave events. Handle client disconnections gracefully by removing them from rooms and notifying others. Include a /rooms endpoint that returns the list of active rooms and their user counts.
problem_hints: Maintain a Hub struct with rooms map[string]map[*Client]bool. Clients register/unregister through channels the Hub listens on.
Each Client has a goroutine for reading (readPump) and one for writing (writePump). Messages are sent to the client's send channel.
On disconnect, the readPump exits, triggering unregister. The Hub removes the client from their room and broadcasts a leave event.

problem_rubric.description: Upgrade works. Read/write pumps handle messages. Ping/pong keepalive.
Multiple rooms work. Messages only go to same-room clients. Join/leave commands work.
Messages broadcast to all room members except sender. System events for join/leave.
Graceful cleanup on disconnect. Other users notified. No goroutine leaks.
HTTP endpoint returns active rooms with user counts as JSON.

problem_description: Create a data pipeline framework using Go channels. Implement a Pipeline struct that chains together processing stages. Each stage is a function that takes an input channel and returns an output channel. Build these stages: a Generator that produces items, a Filter that passes only items matching a predicate, a Transform that maps items through a function, a FanOut that distributes work to N parallel workers, a FanIn that merges N channels into one, and a Sink that collects final results. Use context for cancellation throughout. Demonstrate with a pipeline that generates numbers 1-1000, filters evens, squares them, processes in 4 parallel workers, and collects results.
problem_hints: Each stage is func(ctx context.Context, in <-chan T) <-chan T. It launches a goroutine that reads from in and writes to a new output channel.
FanOut creates N copies of a stage, each reading from the same input channel. FanIn uses sync.WaitGroup and a merged output channel.
Always select on ctx.Done() alongside channel operations to support cancellation. Close output channels when input is exhausted.

problem_rubric.description: Generator, Filter, Transform, Sink all work correctly as channel-based stages.
FanOut distributes to N workers. FanIn merges without deadlock or data loss.
Stages chain together cleanly. Pipeline is reusable with different stages.
All stages respect context cancellation. No goroutine leaks on cancel.
Example pipeline produces correct results (squared even numbers from 1-1000).

problem_description: Implement a REST API for a task management system with full CRUD operations backed by SQLite. Use database/sql with the go-sqlite3 driver. Design a tasks table with id, title, description, status (todo/in_progress/done), priority (low/medium/high), created_at, and updated_at. Implement endpoints: GET /tasks (with query params for filtering by status and sorting), GET /tasks/{id}, POST /tasks, PUT /tasks/{id}, DELETE /tasks/{id}. Use prepared statements for all queries. Implement proper database migrations on startup. Return paginated results with total count, page, and per_page metadata.
problem_hints: Run CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS on startup for migration. Use db.Prepare for prepared statements stored on your repository struct.
For filtering and sorting, dynamically build the WHERE clause and ORDER BY based on query params. Be careful to avoid SQL injection even with dynamic queries.
Pagination: SELECT COUNT(*) for total, then SELECT ... LIMIT ? OFFSET ?. Return metadata as { data: [...], total: N, page: X, per_page: Y }.

problem_rubric.description: SQLite setup, migrations, prepared statements, and connection management are correct.
All five endpoints work correctly with proper status codes and validation.
Query param filtering by status and sorting by fields work. SQL injection prevented.
Results are paginated. Metadata includes total, page, per_page.
404 for missing tasks. 400 for invalid input. 500 for DB errors with safe messages.

problem_description: Build a reverse proxy server with load balancing in Go. The proxy should accept a list of backend server URLs from a config file. Implement three load balancing strategies: round-robin, least-connections, and random. The proxy should forward incoming HTTP requests to a selected backend, copy all headers, stream the response back to the client, and handle backend failures by retrying on the next available server. Implement health checking: periodically ping each backend's /health endpoint and remove unhealthy backends from the rotation. Add request/response logging middleware and support for configurable timeouts on backend connections.
problem_hints: Use httputil.NewSingleHostReverseProxy as a base or implement forwarding manually with http.Client and copying headers.
For least-connections, track active connections per backend with atomic counters. Increment on forward, decrement when response completes.
Health checker: a goroutine per backend that ticks every N seconds and sends GET /health. Set a healthy boolean flag atomically. Load balancers skip unhealthy backends.

problem_rubric.description: Requests forwarded correctly. Headers and body preserved. Response streamed back.
All three strategies implemented and selectable. Distribution is correct.
Periodic health checks. Unhealthy backends removed. Healthy ones re-added.
Failed backends trigger retry on next server. Proper timeout handling.
Config file parsed. Timeouts configurable. Logging middleware works.

problem_description: Implement a distributed task scheduler that coordinates work across multiple worker nodes. The scheduler exposes an HTTP API: POST /tasks submits a task (with type, payload, scheduled_at, and max_retries), GET /tasks/{id} returns status, and GET /tasks returns all tasks with filtering. Workers poll GET /tasks/next to claim the next available task (using optimistic locking to prevent double-claiming). When a worker claims a task, it has a configurable timeout to complete it. If the timeout expires, the task is marked as failed and re-queued up to max_retries times. Track task state transitions: pending -> claimed -> running -> completed|failed. Store everything in SQLite with proper transactions.
problem_hints: Optimistic locking: UPDATE tasks SET status='claimed', worker_id=?, claimed_at=? WHERE id=? AND status='pending' and check rows affected.
Use a background goroutine to check for tasks stuck in 'claimed' or 'running' beyond the timeout. Reset them to 'pending' if retries remain, 'failed' otherwise.
Wrap claim + return in a transaction. Use FOR UPDATE or check RowsAffected to ensure only one worker claims each task.

problem_rubric.description: POST creates tasks in DB. All fields stored. GET endpoints return correct data.
Optimistic locking prevents double-claims. Only one worker gets each task.
Stuck tasks detected and requeued. Max retries respected. Failed state is terminal.
All state transitions are valid. No illegal transitions. History tracked.
DB transactions used correctly. Concurrent workers don't cause corruption.

problem_description: Build a real-time event streaming system using Server-Sent Events (SSE). Implement an event bus that supports multiple named channels. Clients connect via GET /events/{channel} and receive a stream of SSE-formatted events. Publishers send events via POST /events/{channel} with JSON payloads. Support event types, IDs for resumption (Last-Event-ID header), and event replay from a bounded in-memory history buffer (last 1000 events per channel). Handle client disconnections via context cancellation. Implement backpressure: if a client's send buffer is full, skip events for that client with a warning. Include a dashboard endpoint GET /dashboard that returns stats (connected clients per channel, events per second, total events).
problem_hints: Use http.Flusher interface to flush after each event. Check if w implements Flusher. Use r.Context().Done() to detect client disconnect.
Store events in a circular buffer per channel. On new connection, check Last-Event-ID header and replay events after that ID before switching to live stream.

problem_rubric.description: Correct SSE format with id, event, data fields. Proper headers and flushing.
Multiple channels. Publishers and subscribers work independently. Clean routing.
History buffer stores last 1000 events. Last-Event-ID triggers replay of missed events.
Slow clients skipped. Disconnected clients cleaned up. No goroutine leaks.
Stats endpoint shows per-channel clients, events/sec, and totals.

problem_description: Implement a circuit breaker pattern as a Go library. The circuit breaker wraps function calls and monitors failures. It has three states: Closed (normal operation, tracking failure count), Open (all calls rejected immediately, returning a fast-fail error), and Half-Open (allowing a limited number of probe requests to test recovery). Configure thresholds: failure count to trip open, timeout before transitioning to half-open, and success count in half-open to close again. Implement the library as a generic wrapper that works with any function signature using generics. Provide callback hooks for state transitions. Include a comprehensive test suite that simulates failure scenarios, state transitions, concurrent access, and recovery patterns.
problem_hints: States: Closed tracks consecutive failures. When failures >= threshold, transition to Open with a timer. When timer expires, go to HalfOpen.
Use sync.RWMutex for state access. The Execute method checks state: Open returns error immediately, Closed/HalfOpen execute the function and update counters.
For generics: type CircuitBreaker[T any] struct. Execute takes func() (T, error) and returns (T, error). State transition callbacks: OnStateChange func(from, to State).

problem_rubric.description: Three states implemented correctly. All transitions follow circuit breaker specification.
Thresholds configurable. Timeout, failure count, and success count all work.
Works with any function via generics. Clean Execute interface.
State transition callbacks fire correctly. Current state is queryable.
Tests cover all states, transitions, concurrent access, timeout recovery, and edge cases.

problem_description: Build a file synchronization service. The server exposes an API for clients to upload files, download files, and list files with metadata (name, size, checksum, last_modified). Implement chunked file upload: large files are split into 1MB chunks, uploaded individually with chunk index, and reassembled on the server. Use SHA-256 checksums to verify integrity at both chunk and whole-file level. Support resumable uploads: if an upload is interrupted, the client can query which chunks have been received and resume from where it left off. Implement a diff endpoint that accepts a list of local file checksums and returns which files need to be uploaded, downloaded, or deleted to synchronize. Store file metadata in SQLite and file contents on disk.
problem_hints: Store chunks in a temp directory keyed by upload ID. Track received chunks in the DB. On final assembly, concatenate chunks in order and verify the whole-file checksum.

For resumable uploads: POST /uploads to start (returns upload_id), PUT /uploads/{id}/chunks/{index} for each chunk, GET /uploads/{id}/status to see which chunks are received, POST /uploads/{id}/complete to assemble.
The diff endpoint compares client checksums against server checksums. Files only on client need upload, only on server need download, and checksums that differ need update.

problem_rubric.description: Files split into chunks. Chunks uploaded individually. Assembly produces correct file.
SHA-256 checksums verified per-chunk and whole-file. Corrupt chunks rejected.
Status endpoint reports received chunks. Client can resume from last successful chunk.
Diff endpoint correctly identifies files to upload, download, and delete.
SQLite metadata and disk storage work correctly. File listing with metadata works.

problem_description: Create a mini container runtime in Go that demonstrates core Linux container concepts. Implement process isolation using OS-level primitives: use syscall.SysProcAttr to create new namespaces (UTS, PID, mount), set a custom hostname inside the container, mount a proc filesystem, and pivot_root to a provided filesystem directory to give the container its own root filesystem. Implement resource limiting using cgroups v2: set memory limit and CPU quota by writing to cgroup files. The runtime should accept a rootfs path and a command to execute inside the container. Include proper cleanup: unmount filesystems and remove cgroup entries on exit. Print clear status messages for each isolation step.
problem_hints: Use cmd.SysProcAttr = &syscall.SysProcAttr{Cloneflags: syscall.CLONE_NEWUTS | syscall.CLONE_NEWPID | syscall.CLONE_NEWNS} to create namespaces.
Inside the child process: syscall.Sethostname for UTS, syscall.Mount('proc', '/proc', 'proc', 0, '') for proc mount, and pivot_root to change root.
For cgroups v2: write to /sys/fs/cgroup/{container-name}/memory.max and cpu.max. Add the child PID to cgroup.procs. Clean up by removing the cgroup directory on exit.

problem_rubric.description: UTS, PID, and mount namespaces created. Hostname is isolated. PID 1 inside container.
pivot_root changes root filesystem. Proc mounted. Provided rootfs used correctly.
Memory limit and CPU quota set via cgroups v2. Limits are enforced.
Filesystems unmounted. Cgroup entries removed. No resource leaks on exit.
Clear status messages for each step. Errors reported with context. Usage help available.

problem_description: Write a GPIO driver module for an ARM Cortex-M microcontroller. Implement functions to configure a pin as input or output, set a pin high or low, read a pin state, and toggle a pin. Use memory-mapped I/O by defining register addresses as volatile pointers. The driver should accept a port base address and pin number (0-15) and manipulate the correct bits in the direction register (DDR), output register (PORT), and input register (PIN). Do not use any vendor HAL libraries.
problem_hints: Memory-mapped registers are accessed via volatile pointers: #define GPIO_PORT_DIR (*(volatile uint32_t *)(base + 0x00)).
To set bit N: register |= (1 << N). To clear bit N: register &= ~(1 << N). To toggle: register ^= (1 << N).
Use volatile uint32_t* for all register accesses. Cast the base address and add offsets for DIR, OUT, and IN registers.

problem_rubric.description: Correct use of volatile pointers for memory-mapped I/O. Proper base + offset addressing.
Set, clear, toggle, and read operations use correct bitwise operations on the right pin.
Clean function signatures accepting port base and pin number. Input/output config works.
Pin number bounds checking. No undefined behavior. volatile used correctly.

problem_description: Implement a circular (ring) buffer library in C for buffering UART data. The buffer should work with a fixed-size statically allocated array (no malloc). Implement functions: ring_buf_init, ring_buf_put (returns error if full), ring_buf_get (returns error if empty), ring_buf_is_full, ring_buf_is_empty, and ring_buf_count. The buffer must be safe for single-producer single-consumer use without locks by using head and tail indices correctly. Size must be a power of 2 to allow efficient modulo via bitmask.
problem_hints: Use head for write position and tail for read position. The buffer is empty when head == tail, full when ((head + 1) & mask) == tail.
Power-of-2 size allows replacing modulo with bitmask: index & (size - 1) instead of index % size.
For SPSC safety, only the producer modifies head and only the consumer modifies tail. No lock needed if using volatile or appropriate memory barriers.

problem_rubric.description: Put, get, full, empty, and count all work correctly.
Wrap-around works. Bitmask used for efficient modulo. No off-by-one errors.
No dynamic memory. Fixed-size array. Power-of-2 enforcement.
Safe for single-producer single-consumer without locks. Correct index discipline.

problem_description: Write a software debouncing module for mechanical push buttons. Implement a debounce algorithm that samples a button's GPIO state at regular intervals (e.g., every 5ms via a timer tick) and only reports a state change after the signal has been stable for a configurable number of consecutive samples (e.g., 4). The module should support multiple buttons (up to 8) tracked simultaneously via a struct array. Provide callbacks for button press and release events. Detect and report both short press and long press (held > 1 second).
problem_hints: For each button, maintain a history counter. On each sample, if the raw state matches the last stable state, reset counter. If different, increment counter.
When counter reaches the threshold, update the stable state and fire the appropriate callback (press or release).
For long press detection, start a timer when a press is detected. If the button is still held after 1 second worth of samples, fire the long-press callback.

problem_rubric.description: Consecutive-sample algorithm correctly filters noise. Configurable threshold.
Up to 8 buttons tracked independently in a struct array.
Press and release callbacks fire at correct times. No false triggers.
Long press detected after configurable hold time. Distinguishes short vs long.

problem_description: Implement a UART transmit and receive driver using polling and interrupt-driven modes. For polling mode, implement uart_putc that spins on the transmit-ready flag and uart_getc that spins on the receive-ready flag. For interrupt mode, implement a TX ISR that pulls from a transmit ring buffer and an RX ISR that pushes into a receive ring buffer. Provide uart_init to configure baud rate by calculating the divisor from a given system clock and desired baud rate. Support 8N1 configuration (8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit).
problem_hints: Baud rate divisor = system_clock / (16 * baud_rate) for a standard 16x oversampling UART.
In interrupt mode, the TX ISR checks the ring buffer: if data available, write to TX data register; if empty, disable TX interrupt.
The RX ISR reads from the RX data register and pushes into the RX ring buffer. If the buffer is full, either drop the byte or set an overflow flag.

problem_rubric.description: uart_putc and uart_getc correctly poll status flags and transfer data.
TX and RX ISRs correctly interact with ring buffers and hardware registers.
Divisor calculated correctly. uart_init sets up registers for 8N1.
Ring buffers used for ISR data. No data loss under normal conditions.
Shared variables are volatile. ISRs are kept short. Critical sections handled.

problem_description: Create a timer/counter driver module that configures a hardware timer for three modes: one-shot delay, periodic interrupt, and PWM output. For one-shot mode, configure the timer to fire a single interrupt after a specified number of milliseconds. For periodic mode, fire an interrupt repeatedly at a configurable frequency. For PWM mode, generate a square wave with configurable frequency and duty cycle (0-100%). Implement a millisecond tick counter using the periodic mode that provides a millis() function similar to Arduino. All timing calculations should derive from a configurable system clock frequency.
problem_hints: Timer count = (system_clock / prescaler) * desired_period_seconds. Choose prescaler to keep count within the timer's bit width.
For PWM, set the period register for frequency and the compare register for duty cycle: compare = period * duty_cycle / 100.
millis() reads a volatile uint32_t counter incremented by a 1ms periodic timer ISR. Make the counter volatile and handle 32-bit overflow.

problem_rubric.description: Timer fires once after specified delay. ISR executes callback. Timer stops after.
Timer fires repeatedly at correct frequency. ISR callback invoked each time.
Correct frequency and duty cycle. Duty cycle adjustable 0-100%.
Millisecond counter is accurate and handles overflow.
All timing derived from system clock. Prescaler selection is correct.

problem_description: Implement a finite state machine (FSM) framework in C. Define a state machine struct that holds the current state, a table of state-transition rules, and optional entry/exit action callbacks per state. Transitions are triggered by events. Each rule specifies: current_state, event, next_state, guard condition (function pointer returning bool), and transition action. Implement fsm_init, fsm_dispatch(event), and fsm_get_state. Demonstrate the framework by modeling a traffic light controller with states (Red, Green, Yellow) and events (timer_expired, emergency_stop, emergency_clear).
problem_hints: The transition table is an array of structs: { state_t from, event_t event, state_t to, guard_fn guard, action_fn action }.
fsm_dispatch loops through the table looking for a matching (current_state, event) pair where the guard returns true (or is NULL).
On transition: call current state's exit action, call the transition action, update current state, call new state's entry action.

problem_rubric.description: Generic framework with state, event, transition table, guards, and actions.
Event dispatch finds correct transition. Guard conditions evaluated. Actions fire in order.
State entry and exit callbacks fire during transitions.
All states and transitions modeled correctly. Emergency events work.

problem_description: Write a CRC-16 and CRC-32 calculation library optimized for embedded systems. Implement both a bit-by-bit calculation (minimal RAM) and a lookup-table-based calculation (faster, uses 256-entry or 512-byte table). The lookup table should be generated at compile time using a const array or a generation function called at init. Support CRC-16-CCITT (polynomial 0x1021) and CRC-32 (polynomial 0x04C11DB7). Provide functions to calculate CRC over a byte buffer and an incremental API that can process data in chunks. Verify results against known test vectors (e.g., CRC-32 of the string '123456789' should be 0xCBF43926).
problem_hints: Bit-by-bit: for each bit, shift CRC left. If the shifted-out bit XOR the input bit is 1, XOR CRC with the polynomial.
Table-based: crc = (crc << 8) ^ table[((crc >> 8) ^ byte) & 0xFF] for CRC-16. Pre-compute table[i] by running the bit-by-bit algorithm for byte value i.
Incremental API: pass the running CRC as a parameter. crc_update(crc, data, len) returns the updated CRC. Final CRC may need XOR with 0xFFFFFFFF for CRC-32.

problem_rubric.description: Both bit-by-bit and table-based methods produce correct results for CRC-16 and CRC-32.
Table generated correctly. Stored in const/ROM. Matches expected values.
Chunked processing produces same result as single-buffer calculation.
Known test vectors pass. Both CRC-16-CCITT and CRC-32 verified.

problem_description: Implement an SPI master driver that supports full-duplex communication with configurable clock polarity (CPOL), clock phase (CPHA), bit order (MSB/LSB first), and clock speed via prescaler. Provide functions for: spi_init(config), spi_transfer_byte (sends and receives one byte simultaneously), spi_transfer_buffer (sends/receives an array), and chip select management (assert/deassert GPIO). Implement a higher-level function to communicate with a specific SPI device: read the WHO_AM_I register of an accelerometer by sending the register address with the read bit set and clocking in the response byte. Handle SPI bus arbitration if multiple devices share the bus.
problem_hints: CPOL sets idle clock level. CPHA sets sample edge. Mode 0 = CPOL=0,CPHA=0 (sample on rising, shift on falling).
For full-duplex: write TX data to data register, wait for transfer complete flag, read RX data register. This happens simultaneously.
Bus arbitration: use a mutex or busy flag. Assert CS for the target device, perform transfers, then deassert CS and release the bus.

problem_rubric.description: CPOL, CPHA, bit order, and clock prescaler all configurable and set correctly in registers.
Byte and buffer transfers work in full-duplex. TX and RX data correct.
CS assert/deassert managed correctly per transaction.
Accelerometer WHO_AM_I read implemented correctly with read bit protocol.
Multiple devices can share the bus without conflicts.

problem_description: Build an ADC driver with DMA support for continuous multi-channel sampling. Configure the ADC to scan multiple channels (e.g., 4 analog inputs) in sequence. Set up a DMA transfer to automatically move ADC conversion results into a memory buffer without CPU intervention. Use double-buffering (ping-pong): while DMA fills one buffer, the application processes the other. Implement a callback that fires when each buffer is full. Apply a simple digital low-pass filter (exponential moving average) to the raw samples. Calculate and expose the filtered values in millivolts assuming a 3.3V reference and 12-bit ADC resolution.
problem_hints: ADC scan mode converts channels in sequence. DMA circular mode continuously fills the buffer. Half-transfer and transfer-complete interrupts support double-buffering.
Exponential moving average: filtered = alpha * new_sample + (1 - alpha) * filtered. Use fixed-point: filtered = (alpha * new + (256 - alpha) * filtered) >> 8 with alpha as uint8_t.
Millivolt conversion: mv = (raw * 3300) / 4095 for 12-bit ADC with 3.3V reference. Be careful with integer overflow: use uint32_t for the multiplication.

problem_rubric.description: Multi-channel scan mode configured correctly. Channels convert in sequence.
DMA transfers ADC results to memory. Circular mode. No CPU involvement in transfers.
Ping-pong buffers work. Processing and filling happen concurrently. Callbacks fire correctly.
EMA filter applied correctly using fixed-point math. Smoothing is effective.
Raw to millivolt conversion is accurate. No integer overflow.

problem_description: Implement an I2C master driver that supports standard mode (100kHz) and fast mode (400kHz). Implement the full I2C protocol: generating start/repeated-start conditions, sending address bytes with R/W bit, transmitting and receiving data bytes, sending ACK/NACK, and generating stop conditions. Build higher-level functions: i2c_write_register(device_addr, reg_addr, data, len) and i2c_read_register(device_addr, reg_addr, buffer, len) that handle the complete transaction sequence. Implement bus error detection (arbitration lost, NACK received) with proper recovery. Support clock stretching by checking the SCL line state. Demonstrate by reading temperature from a simulated I2C temperature sensor.
problem_hints: Write register: START, send device_addr+W, send reg_addr, send data bytes, STOP. Read register: START, send device_addr+W, send reg_addr, REPEATED START, send device_addr+R, read data bytes with ACK (NACK on last byte), STOP.
Check the ACK bit after each byte transmission. If NACK received, abort the transaction and return an error code.
Clock stretching: after releasing SCL, wait until SCL actually goes high (the slave may hold it low). Add a timeout to prevent infinite wait.

problem_rubric.description: Start, stop, repeated start, ACK/NACK all generated correctly per I2C spec.
Register read and write sequences are correct. Multi-byte transfers work.
NACK detection, arbitration lost, and bus error recovery implemented.
Standard and fast mode timing configured correctly. Clock stretching handled.
Temperature read from simulated sensor with correct byte order and conversion.

problem_description: Design and implement a cooperative task scheduler for a bare-metal embedded system (no RTOS). Each task is a function pointer with a configurable period in milliseconds. The scheduler maintains a task table (max 16 tasks) and runs tasks when their period has elapsed based on a system tick counter. Implement scheduler_init, scheduler_add_task(task_fn, period_ms, priority), scheduler_remove_task, and scheduler_run (the main loop). Higher-priority tasks run first when multiple tasks are due. Include an idle hook that executes when no tasks are ready. Track worst-case execution time per task and provide a scheduler_stats function.
problem_hints: Each task entry stores: function pointer, period, last_run tick, priority, and wcet fields. scheduler_run loops forever checking which tasks are due.
A task is due when (current_tick - last_run) >= period. Sort or scan by priority to run the highest-priority due task first.

problem_rubric.description: Add and remove tasks correctly. Max 16 enforced. Task table is well-structured.
