problem_description: Implement a power management module that transitions a microcontroller between four power modes: Active, Idle, Sleep, and Deep Sleep. Each mode has different wake-up sources and latencies. In Idle mode, halt the CPU but keep peripherals running. In Sleep mode, disable most clocks but keep the RTC and one GPIO interrupt for wake-up. In Deep Sleep, only the RTC continues. Before entering a low-power mode, save peripheral state to a retention struct. On wake-up, restore the state and reinitialize disabled peripherals. Implement an API that accepts a minimum sleep duration and automatically selects the deepest sleep mode that can wake up in time. Track total time spent in each mode.
problem_hints: Create a retention struct that stores the configuration registers of peripherals that lose state in deep sleep.
Mode selection: if sleep_duration < idle_threshold, use Idle. If < sleep_threshold, use Sleep. Otherwise Deep Sleep. Account for wake-up latency.
Use the RTC alarm to schedule wake-up. Configure the GPIO interrupt for external wake-up. After wake-up, check the wake-up source register to determine what woke the system.

problem_rubric.description: All four modes implemented with correct clock/peripheral management per mode.
Peripheral state saved before sleep and restored after wake-up correctly.
Deepest suitable mode chosen based on duration and wake-up latency.
Wake-up sources configured. Time tracking per mode is accurate.

problem_description: Build a command-line interface (CLI) shell over UART for an embedded system. The shell should read characters from UART, support line editing (backspace, cursor movement with arrow keys), maintain a command history buffer (last 8 commands, navigable with up/down arrows), and parse commands with arguments. Implement a command registry where modules can register commands with a name, help text, and handler function. Include built-in commands: 'help' (lists all commands), 'info' (prints system info like uptime and free stack), and 'reboot'. Handle escape sequences for arrow keys (ESC [ A/B/C/D). Support tab completion for command names.
problem_hints: Arrow keys send 3-byte escape sequences: ESC (0x1B), '[', then A/B/C/D. Detect ESC and read the next two bytes to determine the key.
Command history is a circular buffer of strings. Up arrow moves back in history, down arrow moves forward. Copy the history entry into the current line buffer.
Tab completion: on TAB, find all registered commands that start with the current input. If one match, complete it. If multiple, print all matches.

problem_rubric.description: Character-by-character input with echo. Backspace and line editing work.
Commands split into name and arguments correctly. Registry lookup works.
Up/down arrows navigate history. Circular buffer stores last 8 commands.
Tab completes unique matches. Shows all options for ambiguous matches.
help, info, and reboot work correctly. Command registration is clean.

problem_description: Implement a flash memory storage driver with wear leveling for storing configuration data on an embedded system. The flash has 4KB sectors that must be erased before writing (erase sets all bits to 1, write can only clear bits to 0). Implement a simple log-structured storage: new writes append to the current sector with a header (key, length, sequence number). To read a key, scan for the latest entry with that key. When a sector is full, compact it by copying only the latest value of each key to a fresh sector and erasing the old one. Track erase counts per sector and rotate to the least-erased sector for wear leveling. Support at least 32 unique keys with values up to 64 bytes each.
problem_hints: Each entry header: 1 byte key_id, 1 byte length, 2 byte sequence number, then data bytes. A key_id of 0xFF means empty (erased) space.
To find the latest value: scan all entries, tracking the highest sequence number seen for each key.
Compaction: allocate a new sector, write only the latest entry per key, erase the old sector, update the active sector pointer. Increment the erased sector's wear count.

problem_rubric.description: Sector erase and byte-write semantics respected. No invalid operations.
Append writes with headers. Read scans for latest sequence number. Correct results.
Compaction copies latest values to new sector. Old sector erased. No data loss.
Erase counts tracked. Least-worn sector chosen for new writes.
Handles full sectors, power loss during compaction (basic), and max keys/sizes.

problem_description: Create a lightweight memory pool allocator for an embedded RTOS environment where malloc/free are not available or too slow. Implement fixed-size block pools: pool_create(block_size, num_blocks) pre-allocates a static memory region divided into equal blocks. pool_alloc returns a free block in O(1) time, pool_free returns it in O(1) time. Use a free-list linked through the free blocks themselves (the first bytes of a free block store the pointer to the next free block). Support multiple pools of different sizes. Implement a multi-pool allocator that selects the smallest pool whose block size fits the request. Add debug features: detect double-free, detect buffer overflow via sentinel bytes, and report pool utilization stats.
problem_hints: Initialize the free list by linking all blocks: each block's first sizeof(void*) bytes point to the next block. The last block points to NULL.
pool_alloc pops the head of the free list. pool_free pushes to the head. Both are O(1). Use a critical section or disable interrupts for thread safety.
Sentinel bytes: write a magic pattern (e.g., 0xDEADBEEF) after each block's usable area. On free, check if the sentinel is intact. If not, overflow detected.

problem_rubric.description: Fixed-size blocks allocated from static memory. Free list works correctly. O(1) alloc/free.
Multiple pool sizes. Best-fit selection. Fallback when preferred pool is empty.
Critical sections protect free list. Safe for use from multiple RTOS tasks.
Double-free detection, overflow sentinels, and utilization stats all work.

problem_description: Implement a bootloader for an ARM Cortex-M microcontroller. The bootloader resides in the first 16KB of flash and the application starts at 0x4000. On reset, the bootloader checks if a firmware update is available (flag in a dedicated flash page). If no update, it jumps to the application by reading the application's vector table (initial stack pointer at 0x4000 and reset handler at 0x4004). If an update is available, receive the new firmware image over UART using XMODEM protocol (128-byte packets with CRC-16 checksum). Verify the complete image with a CRC-32 before writing to application flash. Erase only the necessary sectors before programming. Implement a rollback mechanism: if the new firmware fails to boot (detected via a watchdog timeout), restore the previous firmware from a backup region.
problem_hints: To jump to app: set MSP to value at 0x4000, then call the function pointer at 0x4004. Disable interrupts and reset peripherals first.
XMODEM: wait for NAK to start, receive SOH + block_num + ~block_num + 128 data bytes + CRC-16. Send ACK for good packets, NAK for bad.
Rollback: before writing new firmware, copy current app to a backup flash region. Set a 'boot_attempt' counter in flash. If the counter exceeds threshold (app didn't clear it), restore from backup.

problem_rubric.description: Correctly reads vector table and jumps to app. MSP set. Interrupts disabled before jump.
Full XMODEM protocol with CRC-16. Handles retries, timeouts, and cancellation.
Correct erase-then-write sequence. Only necessary sectors erased. CRC-32 verified before commit.
Backup created. Boot counter tracks attempts. Automatic rollback on failure.
Bootloader cannot be overwritten. Power loss during update is recoverable.

problem_description: Design and implement a priority-based preemptive task scheduler as a minimal RTOS kernel. Support up to 8 tasks, each with its own stack space. Implement context switching using PendSV exception on ARM Cortex-M: save registers (R4-R11) to the current task's stack, switch to the next task's stack, and restore registers. Each task has a priority level. The highest-priority ready task runs. Implement a SysTick handler for time slicing among equal-priority tasks. Provide kernel APIs: task_create(function, stack, stack_size, priority), task_delay(ticks), mutex_create, mutex_lock (with priority inheritance to prevent priority inversion), and mutex_unlock. Implement the idle task that runs when no other tasks are ready.
problem_hints: PendSV saves R4-R11 manually. R0-R3, R12, LR, PC, xPSR are saved automatically by the exception entry. Store/restore PSP for each task.
Task states: READY, RUNNING, BLOCKED, DELAYED. task_delay moves task to DELAYED with a wake-up tick count. SysTick decrements delays and moves tasks back to READY.
Priority inheritance: when a low-priority task holds a mutex that a high-priority task wants, temporarily boost the holder's priority to the waiter's level. Restore on unlock.

problem_rubric.description: PendSV correctly saves and restores R4-R11 and PSP. Tasks resume correctly.
Highest-priority ready task runs. Time-slicing for equal priority via SysTick.
task_create, task_delay work. Task states tracked correctly. Idle task runs when appropriate.
Mutex lock/unlock work. Priority inheritance prevents inversion. Priority restored on unlock.
Each task has dedicated stack. Initial stack frame set up correctly for first context switch.

problem_description: Implement a real-time digital signal processing pipeline on an embedded system. The pipeline consists of: (1) an ADC ISR that fills a double-buffered input at 44.1kHz sample rate, (2) a 64-tap FIR low-pass filter with configurable coefficients, (3) a fast 256-point FFT (radix-2 decimation-in-time) using fixed-point Q15 arithmetic, and (4) a peak detector that identifies the dominant frequency in the spectrum. All DSP operations must use fixed-point math (no floating point). The FIR filter should use a circular buffer to avoid shifting the sample array. Optimize the FFT with bit-reversal permutation and butterfly operations. Output the dominant frequency and its magnitude via UART at 10Hz update rate.
problem_hints: Q15 format: multiply two Q15 values and shift right 15. Use int32_t for intermediate results to avoid overflow: result = (int32_t)a * b >> 15.
FIR with circular buffer: maintain a write index. On new sample, write at index, then compute output = sum(coeffs[i] * buffer[(write_index - i) & mask]). Bitmask for power-of-2 buffer.
FFT butterfly: for each stage s, step = 2^s, half = step/2. For each group, apply: temp = twiddle * odd; even' = even + temp; odd' = even - temp. Pre-compute twiddle factors as Q15.

problem_rubric.description: ISR fills buffers at 44.1kHz. Ping-pong works. No data loss.
64-tap FIR with circular buffer. Fixed-point arithmetic correct. Coefficients configurable.
256-point radix-2 FFT in Q15. Bit-reversal and butterfly operations correct.
Dominant frequency identified correctly from FFT magnitude spectrum.
All operations use Q15. No overflow. Results accurate within acceptable tolerance.

problem_description: Implement a lightweight TCP/IP stack for an embedded system with an Ethernet MAC peripheral. Implement the following layers: (1) Ethernet frame parsing and construction (source/destination MAC, EtherType), (2) ARP protocol (request/reply, ARP cache table with timeout), (3) IPv4 (header construction/parsing, checksum calculation, basic routing to default gateway), (4) ICMP echo (respond to pings), and (5) a minimal UDP layer (send and receive datagrams on configurable ports with a callback-based API). All buffers must be statically allocated from a fixed-size buffer pool. Implement the IP header checksum using the ones-complement sum algorithm. The stack should handle at least 4 concurrent UDP sockets.
problem_hints: IP checksum: sum all 16-bit words of the header, fold carries (add high 16 bits to low 16 bits), then invert. Do not include the checksum field itself (set to 0 before calculating).
ARP: on outgoing packet, check ARP cache for destination MAC. If not found, queue the packet, send ARP request, and transmit the queued packet when the reply arrives.
Buffer pool: pre-allocate an array of fixed-size (e.g., 1536 byte) buffers. Alloc/free use a free list. Each layer adds/strips its header by adjusting a data pointer within the buffer.

problem_rubric.description: Frame parsing and construction correct. MAC addresses handled. EtherType dispatching works.
ARP request/reply work. Cache stores entries with timeout. Queued packets sent after resolution.
IP headers correct with valid checksum. ICMP echo replies work. Basic routing to gateway.
Send/receive datagrams. Port-based demux. Callback API. 4 concurrent sockets supported.
Static buffer pool. No dynamic allocation. Zero-copy header manipulation where possible.

problem_description: Build a motor control system that implements Field-Oriented Control (FOC) for a three-phase BLDC motor. Implement: (1) Clarke transform to convert three-phase currents (Ia, Ib, Ic) to two-phase stationary frame (Ialpha, Ibeta), (2) Park transform to convert stationary frame to rotating frame (Id, Iq) using the rotor electrical angle, (3) dual PI controllers for Id (flux) and Iq (torque) current loops, (4) inverse Park transform to convert Vd, Vq back to Valpha, Vbeta, (5) Space Vector PWM (SVPWM) to generate three-phase PWM duty cycles from Valpha, Vbeta. The control loop must run at 20kHz from a timer ISR. Implement a simple six-step rotor position estimator using Hall sensor inputs. Use fixed-point Q15 math for all trigonometric calculations with a lookup table for sin/cos.
problem_hints: Clarke: Ialpha = Ia; Ibeta = (Ia + 2*Ib) / sqrt(3). Park: Id = Ialpha*cos(theta) + Ibeta*sin(theta); Iq = -Ialpha*sin(theta) + Ibeta*cos(theta).
PI controller: output = Kp * error + Ki * integral. Clamp integral to prevent windup. Kp and Ki are in Q15 fixed-point.
SVPWM: determine the sector from Valpha/Vbeta angle, calculate T1 and T2 times for adjacent vectors, distribute the null vector time equally. Convert to duty cycles for three half-bridges.

problem_rubric.description: Forward and inverse transforms mathematically correct in fixed-point.
Id and Iq loops regulate correctly. Anti-windup implemented. Tunable gains.
Sector identification, vector timing, and duty cycle calculation are correct.
20kHz ISR execution. All calculations complete within the ISR period.
Hall sensor decoding gives correct electrical angle. Sin/cos lookup table accurate.

problem_description: Implement a basic Block struct and a Blockchain struct in Rust. Each Block contains an index, timestamp, data string, previous block hash, nonce, and its own hash. Implement a calculate_hash method that concatenates all fields and produces a SHA-256 hash. The Blockchain struct holds a Vec<Block> and provides methods: new() (creates a genesis block), add_block(data), and is_valid() (verifies each block's hash and the chain linkage). Use the sha2 crate for hashing.
problem_hints: Use the sha2 crate: Sha256::new(), hasher.update(data), hasher.finalize(). Convert the result to a hex string with format!.
Genesis block has index 0, previous_hash of '0', and arbitrary data. Each new block's previous_hash must match the last block's hash.
is_valid iterates from block 1, checking: block.hash == block.calculate_hash() AND block.previous_hash == chain[i-1].hash.

problem_rubric.description: Block struct has all required fields. calculate_hash produces correct SHA-256 output.
Genesis block created. add_block links correctly. Chain grows properly.
is_valid checks hash integrity and chain linkage. Detects tampering.
Proper ownership, borrows, and derive macros. No unnecessary clones.

problem_description: Implement a Merkle Tree in Rust for verifying transaction integrity. Given a list of transaction hashes (as byte arrays), build a binary Merkle tree where each leaf is a transaction hash and each internal node is the SHA-256 hash of its two children concatenated. If the number of leaves is odd, duplicate the last leaf. Implement methods: new(transactions), root() returning the Merkle root hash, and generate_proof(index) that returns the sibling hashes needed to verify a specific transaction. Implement a verify_proof(leaf, proof, root) function that recomputes the root from the leaf and proof.
problem_hints: Build bottom-up: start with leaf hashes, then pair them and hash each pair. Repeat until one root remains.
A proof is a Vec<(Hash, Side)> where Side is Left or Right, indicating which side the sibling is on at each level.
Verification: start with the leaf hash. For each proof element, concatenate (sibling, current) or (current, sibling) based on Side, then hash. Final result should match root.

problem_rubric.description: Merkle tree built correctly. Odd leaf count handled by duplication. Root is correct.
generate_proof returns correct sibling hashes with correct left/right orientation.
verify_proof reconstructs the root from leaf + proof. Matches expected root.
Proper use of enums, Vec, slices. No unnecessary allocations. Clean API.

problem_description: Build a simple cryptocurrency wallet in Rust that generates Ed25519 key pairs, derives addresses from public keys, and signs/verifies messages. Use the ed25519-dalek crate. Implement: generate_keypair() from a random seed, derive_address(public_key) by taking the first 20 bytes of the SHA-256 hash of the public key and encoding as hex, sign_message(secret_key, message) returning a signature, and verify_signature(public_key, message, signature) returning a boolean. Add a function to export/import keys as hex strings. Write tests for the sign-then-verify round trip.
problem_hints: Use ed25519_dalek::SigningKey::generate(&mut OsRng) to create a key pair. The VerifyingKey is derived from SigningKey.
Address derivation: hash the public key bytes with SHA-256, take [0..20], and hex-encode. This is similar to how Ethereum derives addresses.
For hex export: use the hex crate or format! with {:02x}. For import: decode hex string to bytes, then construct SigningKey::from_bytes.

problem_rubric.description: Ed25519 keypair generated correctly using secure randomness.
SHA-256 of public key, truncated to 20 bytes, hex encoded. Deterministic.
Messages signed correctly. Valid signatures verify. Invalid signatures rejected.
Keys serialized to hex and deserialized back correctly.
Round-trip test passes. Invalid signature test passes.

problem_description: Implement a Proof of Work mining algorithm in Rust. Given a block header (previous hash, transactions root, timestamp, nonce), find a nonce such that the SHA-256 hash of the serialized header starts with a configurable number of leading zero bits (difficulty). Implement a mine(header, difficulty) function that increments the nonce until the target is met, returning the valid nonce and hash. Also implement a verify_pow(header, nonce, difficulty) function. Measure and display the hash rate (hashes per second). Support adjustable difficulty and demonstrate how increasing difficulty exponentially increases mining time.
problem_hints: Leading zero bits: the first difficulty/8 bytes of the hash must be 0x00, and the next byte must be less than a threshold based on remaining bits.
Simpler approach: convert hash to a big integer or compare byte-by-byte against a target. Target = max_hash >> difficulty.
For hash rate: record start time, count iterations, calculate hashes_per_second = count / elapsed_seconds.

problem_rubric.description: Nonce search finds a hash meeting the difficulty target. Correct hash calculation.
verify_pow independently confirms the nonce produces a valid hash below target.
Configurable difficulty. Demonstrates exponential time increase with difficulty.
Hash rate measured and displayed accurately.
Clean Rust code. Proper serialization. No panics.

problem_description: Create a transaction model in Rust using the UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output) model similar to Bitcoin. Define structs for TransactionInput (referencing a previous tx hash and output index, with a signature) and TransactionOutput (recipient address and amount). A Transaction contains a Vec of inputs and outputs. Implement: create_coinbase_tx (mining reward with no inputs), create_transaction (selecting UTXOs, creating inputs/outputs, handling change), and validate_transaction (verify that input amounts >= output amounts, all referenced UTXOs exist and are unspent, and signatures are valid). Maintain a UTXO set as a HashMap.
problem_hints: UTXO key: (tx_hash, output_index). On new transaction, remove consumed UTXOs and add new ones.
Change output: if input sum > output sum, create an additional output back to the sender for the difference.
Coinbase tx has an empty inputs vec and a single output with the mining reward. It creates new coins.

problem_rubric.description: Transaction, Input, Output structs well-defined. Hash derivation correct.
UTXO set updated correctly on new transactions. No double-spending possible.
UTXO selection, input/output creation, and change handling all correct.
Amount check, UTXO existence, and signature verification all implemented.
Coinbase transaction correctly creates new coins with no inputs.

problem_description: Implement a BIP-39 mnemonic seed phrase generator and HD wallet key derivation in Rust. Generate a 128-bit or 256-bit entropy, compute the checksum (first 4 or 8 bits of SHA-256 of entropy), append to entropy, and split into 11-bit groups mapped to a 2048-word wordlist. Implement mnemonic_to_seed using PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 with the mnemonic as password and 'mnemonic' + optional passphrase as salt (2048 iterations). From the seed, derive a master key and chain code by HMAC-SHA512 of the seed with key 'Bitcoin seed'. Implement one level of child key derivation.
problem_hints: 11-bit groups: concatenate entropy + checksum bits, then take every 11 bits as an index (0-2047) into the wordlist.
PBKDF2: use the pbkdf2 crate with hmac::Hmac<Sha512>. 2048 iterations. Output is 64 bytes (512 bits).
Master key: HMAC-SHA512(key='Bitcoin seed', data=seed). First 32 bytes = private key, last 32 bytes = chain code.

problem_rubric.description: Entropy generated, checksum appended, 11-bit groups mapped to words correctly.
PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA512 with correct parameters produces valid 64-byte seed.
HMAC-SHA512 derives master private key and chain code from seed.
One level of child key derivation works correctly.
BIP-39 English wordlist used. Checksum validated on import.

problem_description: Build a simple blockchain serialization and networking layer in Rust. Define a wire protocol for exchanging blocks and transactions between peers. Implement serialization and deserialization of blocks and transactions using the serde and bincode crates. Define message types: Ping, Pong, RequestBlock(hash), ResponseBlock(Block), BroadcastTransaction(Transaction), and RequestPeers. Implement a message framing protocol over TCP: each message is prefixed with a 4-byte length header. Build a simple peer that can connect to another peer, send and receive framed messages, and handle each message type with a match-based dispatcher.
problem_hints: Use serde with #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)] and bincode::serialize/deserialize for compact binary encoding.
Message framing: write u32 length as big-endian bytes, then the serialized message bytes. On read, read 4 bytes for length, then read exactly that many bytes.
Use an enum with #[serde(tag = "type")] or a simple enum for message types. The dispatcher matches on the enum variant.

problem_rubric.description: Blocks and transactions serialize/deserialize correctly with bincode. Round-trip works.
All message types defined as enum variants. Clean type-safe design.
Length-prefixed framing works. Partial reads handled. No message corruption.
Peer connects, sends, and receives framed messages over TCP.
Match-based handler processes each message type correctly.

problem_description: Implement a simple smart contract virtual machine in Rust. Define a stack-based bytecode instruction set with operations: PUSH(value), POP, ADD, SUB, MUL, DIV, EQ, LT, GT, JUMP(addr), JUMPIF(addr), STORE(key), LOAD(key), and HALT. The VM has a stack (max depth 256), a key-value storage (HashMap<u64, u64>), a program counter, and gas metering (each instruction costs a configurable amount of gas). Implement execute(bytecode, gas_limit) that returns the final stack state and storage, or an error (stack overflow, stack underflow, out of gas, division by zero, invalid opcode). Write at least 5 test programs demonstrating different features.
problem_hints: Represent instructions as an enum. The VM loop: fetch instruction at PC, match on it, execute, increment PC, decrement gas.
JUMPIF pops the top of stack: if nonzero, set PC to addr. STORE pops value then key from stack and writes to storage.
Gas: define a cost per opcode (e.g., arithmetic = 3, storage = 20, jump = 8). Check remaining gas before each instruction.

problem_rubric.description: All opcodes implemented correctly. Stack operations follow expected semantics.
Program counter advances correctly. Jumps work. Programs execute to completion or error.
Gas decremented per instruction. Out-of-gas halts execution with error.
Stack overflow/underflow, division by zero, invalid opcode all handled as errors.
5+ test programs demonstrate arithmetic, jumps, storage, gas limits, and errors.

problem_description: Implement a fungible token contract in Rust (simulating an ERC-20-like token without an actual blockchain). Define a Token struct with name, symbol, decimals, total_supply, balances (HashMap<Address, u128>), and allowances (HashMap<(Address, Address), u128>). Implement methods: mint(to, amount) (only callable by owner), transfer(from, to, amount), approve(owner, spender, amount), transfer_from(spender, from, to, amount), balance_of(address), and allowance(owner, spender). All operations must check for sufficient balance/allowance and prevent overflow. Emit events (as a Vec<Event> log) for Transfer and Approval. Write comprehensive tests including edge cases like zero transfers, self-transfers, and overflow attempts.
problem_hints: Use u128 for amounts to handle large token supplies. Check balance >= amount before subtracting. Use checked_add/checked_sub for overflow safety.
transfer_from: check allowance >= amount, then decrease allowance and call the internal transfer logic.
Events: define an Event enum with Transfer { from, to, amount } and Approval { owner, spender, amount }. Push to a Vec<Event> on each operation.

problem_rubric.description: Mint, transfer, approve, transfer_from all work correctly.
Insufficient balance/allowance rejected. Overflow prevented. Owner-only mint enforced.
Transfer and Approval events emitted correctly with accurate data.
Approve sets allowance. transfer_from decreases it. Double-approve handled.
Comprehensive tests: normal flow, edge cases, error conditions all covered.

problem_description: Build a Proof of Stake (PoS) validator selection system in Rust. Implement a staking mechanism where validators deposit tokens to participate. The validator selection for each block should be weighted by stake: higher stake means higher probability of being selected. Implement: register_validator(address, stake), unregister_validator(address) with an unbonding period of N blocks, select_validator(block_height) using a deterministic random selection seeded by the previous block hash, slash_validator(address, percentage) to penalize misbehavior by reducing stake, and distribute_rewards(block_height, reward_amount) proportionally to all active validators by stake weight. Track validator state: Active, Unbonding(until_block), Slashed.
problem_hints: Weighted selection: compute total_stake, generate a random number in [0, total_stake) using the block hash as seed, then iterate validators accumulating stake until the random number is covered.
For deterministic randomness, hash (previous_block_hash ++ block_height) and interpret the first 8 bytes as a u64 seed.
Unbonding: on unregister, set state to Unbonding(current_height + N). The validator cannot be selected but stake is locked until the unbonding height is reached.

problem_rubric.description: Register/unregister work. Stake tracked per validator. Unbonding period enforced.
Weighted random selection is correct and deterministic for a given seed.
Slash reduces stake by percentage. Validator marked as Slashed. Cannot be selected.
Rewards distributed proportionally to stake. Math is correct with no rounding loss.
Validator states tracked correctly. Transitions are valid.

problem_description: Implement an Automated Market Maker (AMM) DEX in Rust using the constant product formula (x * y = k). Create a LiquidityPool struct that holds reserves of two tokens. Implement: add_liquidity(amount_a, amount_b) that mints LP tokens proportional to the contribution, remove_liquidity(lp_tokens) that burns LP tokens and returns proportional reserves, and swap(token_in, amount_in) that calculates the output amount using the constant product formula with a 0.3% fee. Track LP token balances per address. Implement price_of(token) that returns the current exchange rate. Prevent swaps that would drain more than 90% of any reserve. Write tests verifying the invariant holds after every operation.
problem_hints: Constant product: after swap, new_reserve_in * new_reserve_out >= old_k. Output = reserve_out - (k / (reserve_in + amount_in_after_fee)).
LP tokens on first deposit: mint sqrt(amount_a * amount_b). On subsequent deposits: mint min(amount_a/reserve_a, amount_b/reserve_b) * total_lp_supply.
Fee: amount_in_after_fee = amount_in * 997 / 1000. This keeps 0.3% in the pool, increasing k over time.

problem_rubric.description: Constant product formula applied correctly. Fee deducted. Output amount is accurate.
Add/remove liquidity mints/burns LP tokens proportionally. Reserves update correctly.
k never decreases (only increases from fees). Tests verify after every operation.
Cannot drain >90% of reserve. Zero amounts rejected. Overflow handled.
Exchange rate calculated correctly from current reserves.

problem_description: Build a blockchain-based voting system in Rust. Implement a VotingContract that supports creating proposals, registering voters, casting votes, and tallying results. Each proposal has an ID, description, options list, start_block, and end_block. Voters must be registered before the proposal starts and can only vote once per proposal. Implement vote weight based on token balance at the proposal's start block (snapshot). Support three voting strategies: simple majority, supermajority (66%), and quadratic voting (vote weight = sqrt of token balance). Emit events for ProposalCreated, VoteCast, and ProposalFinalized. Implement a quorum requirement: a minimum percentage of total supply must participate for the result to be valid.
problem_hints: Snapshot: store each voter's balance at proposal creation time. Use this snapshot balance for vote weight, not current balance.
Quadratic voting: weight = integer_sqrt(balance). Implement integer square root with Newton's method or binary search.
Quorum: total_votes_weight / total_snapshot_supply >= quorum_percentage. If not met, proposal result is 'Quorum Not Reached'.

problem_rubric.description: Create proposals with options, time bounds, and voting strategy. Lifecycle works.
Vote casting respects registration, time bounds, and single-vote-per-proposal rule.
Simple majority, supermajority, and quadratic voting all calculate correctly.
Balance snapshot used for weights. Quorum check enforced on finalization.
Events emitted correctly. Tests cover all strategies and edge cases.

problem_description: Implement a blockchain peer-to-peer network simulator in Rust using async Rust (tokio). Create a Network struct that manages multiple Node instances communicating via tokio mpsc channels (simulating network links). Each node maintains its own copy of the blockchain. Implement a gossip protocol: when a node mines or receives a new block, it broadcasts to all connected peers. Implement the longest-chain rule: when a node receives a chain longer than its own, it validates and adopts it. Simulate network partitions by temporarily disconnecting nodes, causing forks, then healing the partition and observing chain convergence. Log all events with timestamps for debugging.
problem_hints: Each Node has a tokio::sync::mpsc::Sender to each peer and a single Receiver for incoming messages. Messages: NewBlock(Block), RequestChain, ResponseChain(Vec<Block>).
Longest chain rule: on receiving a longer valid chain, replace local chain entirely. Validate all blocks in the received chain before adopting.
Network partition: remove the channel connections between two groups of nodes. After some blocks are mined in each partition, reconnect and observe which chain wins.

problem_rubric.description: Tokio mpsc channels connect nodes. Messages sent and received asynchronously.
New blocks propagate to all peers. No message loops. Duplicate blocks ignored.
Nodes adopt longer valid chains. Shorter forks abandoned. Validation before adoption.
Network partition causes forks. Healing leads to convergence on one chain.
Timestamped event logs show block propagation, forks, and convergence.

problem_description: Create an NFT collection system in Rust simulating ERC-721 functionality. Implement an NftCollection struct with: mint(to, metadata_uri) that assigns sequential token IDs, transfer(from, to, token_id), approve(owner, approved, token_id), set_approval_for_all(owner, operator, approved), and owner_of(token_id). Metadata includes a URI, name, description, and attributes array (trait_type/value pairs). Implement enumeration: tokens_of_owner(address) returns all token IDs owned by an address. Add a royalty system: on each transfer, a percentage of a notional sale price is recorded as owed to the original creator. Implement a reveal mechanism: tokens start with a placeholder URI and can be revealed by the collection owner, updating all URIs with a base URI + token ID pattern.
problem_hints: Store owners as HashMap<u64, Address>, approvals as HashMap<u64, Address>, and operator_approvals as HashMap<(Address, Address), bool>.
Transfer checks: caller must be owner, approved, or operator. Update owner map, clear single-token approval on transfer.
Reveal: store a revealed bool and base_uri. Before reveal, token_uri returns placeholder. After reveal, return format!("{}{}", base_uri, token_id).

problem_rubric.description: Mint, transfer, owner_of work correctly. Sequential IDs assigned.
Single approval and operator approval both work. Cleared on transfer.
tokens_of_owner returns correct list. Updated on mint and transfer.
Royalty percentage tracked per collection. Owed amounts accumulate on transfers.
Placeholder before reveal. Base URI + token ID after reveal. Owner-only reveal.

problem_description: Implement a state trie (Modified Merkle Patricia Trie) in Rust for efficiently storing and verifying blockchain account states. The trie should support: insert(key, value), get(key), delete(key), and root_hash() that computes the Merkle root of the entire trie. Implement the three node types: leaf (stores remaining key path + value), extension (stores shared prefix + pointer to child), and branch (16 children + optional value). Keys are nibble-paths (each byte split into two 4-bit nibbles). Compact encoding: store shared prefixes efficiently. Implement generate_proof(key) that returns the nodes along the path for Merkle proof verification.
problem_hints: Split byte keys into nibbles: key 0xAB becomes [0xA, 0xB]. Traversal follows nibble-by-nibble through the trie.
On insert, if a leaf shares a prefix with the new key, split into an extension + branch. If an extension's prefix partially matches, split it.
Root hash: hash leaf as RLP(compact_path, value). Hash branch as RLP(child_hashes[0..15], value). Hash extension as RLP(compact_path, child_hash).

problem_rubric.description: Leaf, extension, and branch nodes implemented correctly. Nibble-path traversal works.
All operations produce correct trie structure. Node splitting on insert works.
Merkle root computed correctly. Changes to any value change the root.
Proof contains correct path nodes. Verification against root succeeds.
Shared prefixes stored efficiently. Nibble paths encoded correctly.

problem_description: Implement a multi-signature wallet contract in Rust. The wallet is controlled by N owners and requires M-of-N signatures to execute any transaction. Implement: create_wallet(owners, required_signatures), submit_transaction(proposer, to, value, data) that creates a pending transaction, confirm_transaction(owner, tx_id) that adds a signature, execute_transaction(tx_id) that executes when enough confirmations are collected, and revoke_confirmation(owner, tx_id). Support adding and removing owners (itself requiring M-of-N approval). Implement a time lock: confirmed transactions must wait a configurable delay before execution. Include a nonce per transaction to prevent replay attacks. Track all transaction states and emit events.
problem_hints: Store pending transactions in a HashMap<u64, PendingTx>. PendingTx has: to, value, data, confirmations: HashSet<Address>, executed: bool, submitted_at: u64.
Execute check: confirmations.len() >= required AND current_block >= submitted_at + timelock_blocks AND !executed.
Owner management: submit a special transaction type (AddOwner/RemoveOwner). It goes through the same M-of-N confirmation flow.

problem_rubric.description: M-of-N confirmation required. Cannot execute with fewer. Cannot confirm twice.
Submit, confirm, execute, revoke all work. State transitions are valid.
Transactions cannot execute before timelock expires. Delay is configurable.
Add/remove owners via M-of-N approval. Required signatures adjustable.
Replay prevention via nonce. Only owners can confirm. Events emitted.

problem_description: Build a simplified Ethereum-like execution environment in Rust. Implement an account-based state model with accounts having nonce, balance, code (bytecode), and storage (HashMap). Implement a transaction processor that handles two transaction types: value transfers (deduct from sender, credit to receiver, increment nonce) and contract calls (load contract code, execute in the VM from problem blockchain_rust_08 or a new simple VM, update storage). Implement gas accounting: each transaction specifies gas_limit and gas_price. Unused gas is refunded. The gas_price * gas_used is paid to the block proposer. Implement transaction ordering by nonce (reject gaps) and a basic mempool that orders pending transactions by gas_price (highest first). Validate transactions: check nonce sequence, sufficient balance for value + gas_limit * gas_price, and valid signatures.
problem_hints: Account state: struct Account { nonce: u64, balance: u128, code: Vec<u8>, storage: HashMap<u64, u64> }. World state is HashMap<Address, Account>.
Transaction validation order: verify signature, check nonce == account.nonce, check balance >= value + gas_limit * gas_price. Then execute.
After execution: actual_cost = gas_used * gas_price. Refund = (gas_limit - gas_used) * gas_price back to sender. Pay actual_cost to proposer.

problem_rubric.description: Account state with nonce, balance, code, storage. World state managed correctly.
Value transfers and contract calls execute correctly. State updates are atomic.
Gas limit enforced. Unused gas refunded. Proposer paid. Out-of-gas reverts state.
Transactions ordered by gas price. Nonce gaps rejected. Sequential execution.
Signature, nonce, and balance checks all enforced before execution.

problem_description: Implement a simplified zero-knowledge proof system in Rust using the Schnorr identification protocol and extend it to a non-interactive proof using the Fiat-Shamir heuristic. First, implement the interactive Schnorr protocol: Prover knows secret x, sends commitment R = g^r (random r), Verifier sends challenge c, Prover responds with s = r + c*x. Verifier checks g^s == R * y^c (where y = g^x is the public key). Then convert to non-interactive by computing c = Hash(g, y, R). Implement this over a prime-order group using the num-bigint crate for big integer arithmetic. Build a higher-level API: prove(secret, message) returning a proof, and verify(public_key, message, proof) returning bool. Demonstrate with a proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm.
problem_hints: Use a safe prime p and generator g of the group Z*_p of order q = (p-1)/2. All arithmetic is mod p.
Fiat-Shamir: c = SHA-256(g || y || R || message) mod q. This makes the proof non-interactive and bound to a specific message.
Proof struct: { R: BigUint, s: BigUint }. Verify: compute c = Hash(...), check g^s mod p == (R * y^c) mod p.

problem_rubric.description: Schnorr identification with commitment, challenge, response implemented correctly.
Non-interactive proof via hashing. Challenge derived deterministically. Message bound.
Modular exponentiation, multiplication correct with big integers. Prime group setup valid.
Clean API. Valid proofs verify. Invalid proofs (wrong secret, wrong message) rejected.
Random nonce r used per proof. No secret leakage. Soundness demonstrated in tests.

problem_description: Build a DeFi lending protocol simulation in Rust. Implement a LendingPool that supports multiple token types. Users can: deposit(token, amount) to supply liquidity and earn interest, withdraw(token, amount) to reclaim deposits plus accrued interest, borrow(collateral_token, borrow_token, amount) using deposited collateral, and repay(token, amount). Implement a collateralization ratio (e.g., 150%): users can only borrow up to collateral_value / ratio. Implement variable interest rates based on utilization (borrowed / total_deposited): low utilization = low rate, high utilization = high rate, using a kinked rate model (two slopes with a kink at 80% utilization). Implement liquidation: when a borrower's collateral ratio falls below 110%, anyone can liquidate by repaying part of the debt and receiving the collateral at a 5% discount. Track accrued interest using a cumulative interest index updated per block.
problem_hints: Interest index: each token has a cumulative_index that grows each block. User's debt = principal * current_index / index_at_borrow_time.
Kinked rate model: if utilization < 80%, rate = base_rate + utilization * slope1. If >= 80%, rate = base_rate + 80% * slope1 + (utilization - 80%) * slope2 (slope2 >> slope1).
Liquidation: liquidator repays up to 50% of borrower's debt. Receives collateral worth (repaid_amount * (1 + discount)) at current prices. Update borrower's debt and collateral.

problem_rubric.description: Supply liquidity and withdraw with accrued interest. Balance tracking correct.
Collateralized borrowing works. Repayment reduces debt. Collateral ratio enforced.
Kinked rate model calculates correct rates. Cumulative index updates per block.
Under-collateralized positions liquidatable. Discount applied. Debt and collateral updated.
Multiple tokens supported. Cross-token borrowing works with price oracle.

problem_description: Implement a complete simplified blockchain node in Rust that integrates all core components. The node should include: (1) a UTXO-based transaction model with signature verification, (2) block creation with Merkle tree transaction root, (3) Proof of Work consensus with adjustable difficulty, (4) a mempool for pending transactions ordered by fee, (5) chain validation and reorganization on receiving a longer valid chain, (6) a simple peer-to-peer layer using tokio TCP for block and transaction propagation between at least 3 nodes, and (7) a JSON-RPC API (using a simple HTTP server) with methods: get_block(hash), get_transaction(hash), get_balance(address), send_transaction(raw_tx), get_mempool, and get_chain_info. The node should handle concurrent mining, transaction reception, and peer communication. Include a difficulty adjustment algorithm that targets one block every 10 seconds, adjusting every 5 blocks.
problem_hints: Structure the node with separate modules: chain (block/tx storage), miner (PoW loop in a spawned task), mempool (pending tx pool), network (peer connections), and rpc (HTTP API).
Use tokio::select! to handle mining, incoming peer messages, and RPC requests concurrently. Mining should be cancellable when a new block is received.
Difficulty adjustment: measure time for last 5 blocks. If < 50s, increase difficulty. If > 50s, decrease. Clamp adjustments to 4x max change per period.

problem_rubric.description: UTXO model with inputs, outputs, signatures. Validation prevents double-spend.
Blocks with Merkle root. PoW mining works. Difficulty adjusts to target.
Chain validation. Reorganization on longer chain. Orphan handling.
P2P block/tx propagation. 3+ nodes communicate. Gossip works.
All RPC methods return correct data. Transactions submittable via API.
All components work together. Concurrent operation without deadlocks.
